subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 13! In this unit you will study probability – the branch of mathematics that measures how likely something is to happen. Every day you already think about chance without noticing. Will it rain before Maghrib? Will Hassan's team win the football match on Friday? If Amina reaches into a bag of dates without looking, will she pull out a soft one or a dry one? Probability gives you a precise, mathematical way to answer questions like these instead of just guessing.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Understand how to find the theoretical probabilities of equally likely outcomes.
Identify all the possible mutually exclusive outcomes of a single event, and recognise when they are equally likely to happen.
Understand and explain that probabilities range from 0 to 1, and can be represented as proper fractions, decimals and percentages.
Recognise that fractions, terminating decimals and percentages have equivalent values.
Design and conduct chance experiments or simulations, using small and large numbers of trials. Analyse the frequency of outcomes to calculate experimental probabilities.
Round numbers to a given number of decimal places.

outcomes: Describe how likely an event is using the words impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely and certain.
Place events on a probability scale from 0 to 1 and read values off it.
Express a probability as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage, and convert between them.
List the sample space – all the possible outcomes – of a simple experiment.
Calculate theoretical probability using P(event) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes.
Use the rule P(not A) = 1 − P(A) to find the probability an event does not happen.
Recognise mutually exclusive events and add their probabilities.

concepts.title: Uncertainty and the Language of Chance
concepts.explanation:
Some things are certain. The sun will rise tomorrow. If today is Thursday, tomorrow will be Friday. Other things are impossible. You cannot roll a 7 on an ordinary six-sided die, because the die only has the faces 1 to 6. But most of life sits somewhere in between these two extremes, in the land of uncertainty. We cannot be sure whether it will rain, whether a seed will sprout, or which side a flipped coin will land on – and that is exactly where probability lives.

Before we use numbers, we use words to describe how likely something is. The five most useful words, from least likely to most likely, are impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely and certain. 'Even chance' means the event is just as likely to happen as not to happen – like a fair coin landing heads. When Farah says a soft rain in the dry season is 'unlikely' and a hot afternoon in Mogadishu is 'likely', she is already thinking like a mathematician, ranking events by how probable they are.

Consider flipping a coin. Even though the coin has only two sides, you cannot say for certain which way it will land. The result depends on the force of the flip, the spin, the air, and the surface it lands on – far too many tiny factors to predict. We call such an event random. Randomness is not the same as chaos: a fair coin still lands heads about half the time. Randomness simply means we cannot predict a single result with certainty, even though a clear pattern appears over many attempts.
concepts.example: Weather forecasting shows this beautifully. When a forecaster says there is a '30% chance of rain', that does not mean it will rain for 30% of the day, nor that 30% of the town will get wet. It means that, out of all the situations that have looked like today, rain has followed in about 30 of every 100. Probability turns a vague feeling of 'maybe' into a clear, comparable number.

concepts.title: The Probability Scale (0 to 1)
concepts.explanation:
Words like 'likely' are useful, but two people may not agree on exactly what they mean. Mathematics gives us something sharper: the probability scale, a number line that runs from 0 to 1. Every probability in the world sits somewhere on this line, and no probability can ever be less than 0 or more than 1.

At the very bottom of the scale, probability 0 means the event is impossible – it can never happen. Rolling a 7 on a standard die has probability 0. At the very top, probability 1 means the event is certain – it must happen. Rolling a number from 1 to 6 on a standard die has probability 1, because every face fits that description. In between, a larger number always means a more likely event.

The exact middle of the scale, probability 1/2 (which is 0.5, or 50%), marks an even chance. A fair coin landing heads sits here. Anything to the left of the middle is unlikely (more likely not to happen than to happen); anything to the right is likely (more likely to happen than not). Picture the scale like a road from Hargeisa to Berbera: 0 at one end, 1 at the other, and the halfway rest-stop at 0.5.

Let us place a few events on the scale to feel how it works. The probability of rolling a 6 on a fair die is 1/6, which is about 0.17 – that sits well to the left, in the 'unlikely' region, because you will fail to roll a 6 more often than you succeed. The probability of picking a weekday if you choose a day of the week at random is 5/7, about 0.71 – that sits to the right, in the 'likely' region. The probability of drawing a red ball from a bag that holds only red balls is 1 – it is certain.
concepts.example: A very important rule follows from all this: a probability can never be bigger than 1 and never smaller than 0. If you ever calculate a probability of 1.5 or −0.2, you have made a mistake somewhere, because those numbers are off the scale. This is one of the fastest ways to check your own work. Whenever you finish a probability calculation, glance at the answer and ask: is it between 0 and 1? If not, go back.

concepts.title: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
concepts.explanation:
The same probability can be written in three equivalent ways: as a fraction, as a decimal, or as a percentage. Each form is useful in different situations, and being able to switch between them quickly is an essential skill in this unit. They are simply three different outfits for the very same number.

A fraction is often the most natural form, because probability is built from a count of favourable outcomes over total outcomes. The probability of rolling a 6 on a die is 1/6, showing directly that there is one favourable face out of six. Fractions keep the structure of the problem visible, which is why we usually calculate in fractions first.

A decimal is handy for comparing probabilities and for calculations. To turn a fraction into a decimal, divide the top by the bottom: 1/6 = 1 ÷ 6 = 0.167 (to three decimal places). Decimals make it easy to see, at a glance, that 0.167 is smaller than 0.25, so a 1/6 chance is less likely than a 1/4 chance.

A percentage is the friendliest form for everyday communication, which is why weather forecasts and news reports nearly always use it. To turn a decimal into a percentage, multiply by 100: 0.167 × 100 = 16.7%. So the three ways of writing the chance of rolling a 6 are 1/6 = 0.167 = 16.7% – all exactly the same likelihood. Here are a few worth memorising: 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%; 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%; 3/4 = 0.75 = 75%; 1/5 = 0.2 = 20%; 1/10 = 0.1 = 10%.
concepts.example: To go the other way, from a percentage back to a fraction, write the percentage over 100 and simplify. A 40% chance is 40/100, which cancels to 2/5. A 25% chance is 25/100 = 1/4. Practise these conversions until they feel automatic, because in real problems you will be asked to move between all three forms freely, sometimes within a single question.

concepts.title: Outcomes, Events and the Sample Space
concepts.explanation:
To calculate probabilities correctly, you first need three precise words. An outcome is a single possible result of an experiment. When you roll a die, the possible outcomes are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. When you flip a coin, the outcomes are heads and tails. An outcome is one thing that could happen on one go.

An event is one or more outcomes that you are interested in. An event can be simple (a single outcome) or compound (several outcomes). 'Rolling a 4' is a simple event, made of just one outcome. 'Rolling an even number' is a compound event, made of the outcomes 2, 4 and 6. The event is the thing you are asking about; the outcomes are the individual results that make it up.

The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes of an experiment. For one die roll, the sample space is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. For one coin flip it is {heads, tails}. For spinning a spinner with four equal colours – red, green, blue, yellow – the sample space is {red, green, blue, yellow}. Listing the sample space carefully is the single most important habit in this unit, because if you miss an outcome, every probability you calculate afterwards will be wrong.

When an experiment has two stages, list the sample space in an organised way so that you catch every combination. Suppose Yusuf flips a coin and rolls a die at the same time. To find all the outcomes, pair each coin result with each die result: H1, H2, H3, H4, H5, H6, T1, T2, T3, T4, T5, T6. That is 2 × 6 = 12 outcomes in the sample space. A table with the coin results down the side and the die results across the top helps you list them without missing any – each cell of the table is one outcome.
concepts.example: Here is another two-stage example that matters for later work. Roll two dice and add the scores. The number of outcomes is 6 × 6 = 36, from (1,1) up to (6,6). But the possible totals run only from 2 to 12, and they are not equally likely. There is just one way to make a total of 2 (a 1 and a 1), but six ways to make a total of 7 (1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1). This is a crucial lesson: to use the probability formula safely, the outcomes you count must be the equally likely ones (the 36 die pairs), not the unequal totals.

concepts.title: Calculating Theoretical Probability
concepts.explanation:
Now we reach the heart of the unit: the formula for theoretical probability. When every outcome is equally likely, the probability of an event is the number of outcomes that make the event happen, divided by the total number of possible outcomes:

P(event) = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of possible outcomes

We call this 'theoretical' because we work it out by pure reasoning about the structure of the experiment, without doing any trials at all. Let us apply it. What is the probability of rolling a 3 on a fair die? There is one favourable outcome (the 3) out of six possible outcomes, so P(3) = 1/6. What about rolling an even number? The favourable outcomes are 2, 4 and 6 – that is three of them – out of six, so P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%. Notice how we simplified the fraction and then wrote it in all three forms.

Consider a bag holding coloured marbles, like the ones Khadija keeps for a game: 4 red, 3 blue and 1 yellow, making 8 marbles in total. If she draws one without looking, P(red) = 4/8 = 1/2, P(blue) = 3/8, and P(yellow) = 1/8. Add them up: 4/8 + 3/8 + 1/8 = 8/8 = 1. This is no accident. When you add the probabilities of every possible outcome of an experiment, they always total 1, because one of them is certain to happen. This gives you another way to check your work.

The formula only works when the outcomes are equally likely – that is, when the experiment is fair. A fair die is equally likely to show any of its six faces. But if a die were weighted or chipped, the faces would no longer be equally likely, and the simple formula would give a wrong answer. In real life, perfect fairness is an ideal: a well-made coin or die is fair enough for our purposes, but always ask yourself whether the equal-likelihood assumption really holds before you use the formula.
concepts.example: Let us try a worded example. In a class at Nuur Academy there are 12 girls and 8 boys, 20 students in all. The teacher picks one name at random to fetch water. What is the probability the chosen student is a girl? Favourable outcomes = 12 (the girls); total outcomes = 20 (everyone). So P(girl) = 12/20 = 3/5 = 0.6 = 60%. And the probability of choosing a boy is 8/20 = 2/5 = 40%. Check: 60% + 40% = 100%, exactly as it should.

concepts.title: The 'Not' Rule and Mutually Exclusive Events
concepts.explanation:
Sometimes it is easier to work out the chance of an event not happening than the chance of it happening. There is a beautiful rule for this. Since all the probabilities in an experiment add up to 1, the probability that an event does not happen is 1 minus the probability that it does:

For example, the probability of rolling a 6 on a die is 1/6, so the probability of not rolling a 6 is 1 − 1/6 = 5/6. This makes sense: five of the six faces are 'not a 6'. The 'not' event is called the complement, and the rule is one of the most useful shortcuts in probability, especially when the event you want is complicated but its opposite is simple. If Omar wants the probability of not drawing the winning raffle ticket, it is far quicker to work out the small chance of winning and subtract from 1.

Now for mutually exclusive events. Two events are mutually exclusive if they cannot both happen at the same time. On a single die roll, 'rolling a 2' and 'rolling a 5' are mutually exclusive – one roll cannot be both a 2 and a 5. When two events are mutually exclusive, the probability that one or the other happens is found by adding their probabilities:

P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) (only when A and B are mutually exclusive)

So the probability of rolling a 2 or a 5 is P(2) + P(5) = 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 = 1/3. Likewise, drawing a marble that is 'red or yellow' from Khadija's bag (4 red, 3 blue, 1 yellow) is 4/8 + 1/8 = 5/8. The addition rule works here because no marble is both red and yellow at once.
concepts.example: Be careful, though: not all events are mutually exclusive, and then you cannot simply add. On a die, 'rolling an even number' and 'rolling a number greater than 3' can happen together, because a 4 or a 6 fits both descriptions. Events that share an outcome overlap, and adding their probabilities would count the shared outcomes twice. For now, always check first: can these two events happen on the same go? If the answer is no, they are mutually exclusive and you may add.

methods.title: How to calculate a theoretical probability
methods.example: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. Find P(rolling a number less than 3), as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage.
steps: List the sample space — every possible outcome.
Count the total number of outcomes.
Count how many outcomes are favourable (make the event happen).
Write P = favourable ÷ total, then simplify the fraction.
Convert to a decimal or percentage if the question asks.

methods.title: How to find an experimental probability
methods.example: A bag holds 5 red, 2 blue and 3 green marbles. One is drawn at random. Find P(red) and P(not red).
steps: Do the experiment many times, keeping conditions the same.
Record every result in a frequency table with a tally.
For each outcome, divide its frequency by the total number of trials.
Compare with the theoretical value if there is one.

methods.title: How to convert between forms
methods.example: A fair die is rolled. Find the probability of rolling a 1 or a 4.
steps: Fraction to decimal: divide the top by the bottom.
Decimal to percentage: multiply by 100.
Percentage to fraction: write it over 100 and simplify.

methods.title: Two-stage sample space
methods.example: A coin is flipped and a die is rolled. List the sample space and find P(heads and an even number).
steps: The sample space has 2 × 6 = 12 equally likely outcomes: H1, H2, H3, H4, H5, H6, T1, T2, T3, T4, T5, T6.
The favourable outcomes (heads with an even number) are H2, H4 and H6 — that is 3.
So P(heads and even) = 3/12 = 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%.

methods.title: Experimental probability
methods.example: Hassan spins a spinner 40 times. It lands on 'star' 16 times. Find the experimental probability of landing on a star, and compare it with a theoretical value of 1/4 for a fair spinner.
steps: Experimental probability = 16/40 = 2/5 = 0.4 = 40%.
The theoretical value is 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%.
The experimental result (40%) is noticeably higher than 25%, but 40 spins is not very many.
To decide whether the spinner is really biased, Hassan should spin it many more times and see whether the relative frequency settles near 25% or stays high.

methods.title: Using the complement to save work
methods.example: A spinner has 10 equal sectors numbered 1 to 10. Find the probability of not landing on a multiple of 5.
steps: The multiples of 5 from 1 to 10 are 5 and 10, so P(multiple of 5) = 2/10 = 1/5.
Using the complement rule, P(not a multiple of 5) = 1 − 1/5 = 4/5 = 0.8 = 80%.
This was quicker than listing the eight other numbers.

workedExamples.title: A single die
workedExamples.prompt: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. Find P(rolling a number less than 3), as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage.
workedExamples.solution: The numbers less than 3 are 1 and 2, so there are 2 favourable outcomes out of 6. P = 2/6 = 1/3. As a decimal, 1 ÷ 3 = 0.33 (to 2 d.p.). As a percentage, 0.33 × 100 = 33% (to the nearest whole). So P(less than 3) = 1/3 ≈ 0.33 ≈ 33%.

workedExamples.title: Marbles in a bag
workedExamples.prompt: A bag holds 5 red, 2 blue and 3 green marbles. One is drawn at random. Find P(red) and P(not red).
workedExamples.solution: Total marbles = 5 + 2 + 3 = 10. P(red) = 5/10 = 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%. For the complement, P(not red) = 1 − 1/2 = 1/2. You can check directly: 'not red' means blue or green = 2 + 3 = 5 out of 10 = 1/2. Both methods agree.

workedExamples.title: Mutually exclusive events
workedExamples.prompt: A fair die is rolled. Find the probability of rolling a 1 or a 4.
workedExamples.solution: 'Rolling a 1' and 'rolling a 4' cannot both happen on one roll, so they are mutually exclusive and we may add. P(1) = 1/6 and P(4) = 1/6, so P(1 or 4) = 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 = 1/3.

workedExamples.title: Two-stage sample space
workedExamples.prompt: A coin is flipped and a die is rolled. List the sample space and find P(heads and an even number).
workedExamples.solution: The sample space has 2 × 6 = 12 equally likely outcomes: H1, H2, H3, H4, H5, H6, T1, T2, T3, T4, T5, T6. The favourable outcomes (heads with an even number) are H2, H4 and H6 — that is 3. So P(heads and even) = 3/12 = 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%.

workedExamples.title: Experimental probability
workedExamples.prompt: Hassan spins a spinner 40 times. It lands on 'star' 16 times. Find the experimental probability of landing on a star, and compare it with a theoretical value of 1/4 for a fair spinner.
workedExamples.solution: Experimental probability = 16/40 = 2/5 = 0.4 = 40%. The theoretical value is 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%. The experimental result (40%) is noticeably higher than 25%, but 40 spins is not very many. To decide whether the spinner is really biased, Hassan should spin it many more times and see whether the relative frequency settles near 25% or stays high.

workedExamples.title: Using the complement to save work
workedExamples.prompt: A spinner has 10 equal sectors numbered 1 to 10. Find the probability of not landing on a multiple of 5.
workedExamples.solution: The multiples of 5 from 1 to 10 are 5 and 10, so P(multiple of 5) = 2/10 = 1/5. Using the complement rule, P(not a multiple of 5) = 1 − 1/5 = 4/5 = 0.8 = 80%. This was quicker than listing the eight other numbers.

workedExamples.title: Total of two dice
workedExamples.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled and the scores are added. Find P(total of 7).
workedExamples.solution: There are 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes. The pairs giving a total of 7 are (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2) and (6,1) — that is 6 favourable outcomes. So P(total of 7) = 6/36 = 1/6. This is why 7 is the most common total when rolling two die.

workedExamples.title: Reasoning backwards
workedExamples.prompt: In a bag of red and yellow sweets, the probability of drawing a red is 3/5. There are 20 sweets in total. How many are red, and how many are yellow?
workedExamples.solution: P(red) = 3/5 means 3 out of every 5 sweets are red. Of 20 sweets, red = 3/5 × 20 = 12. Yellow = 20 − 12 = 8. Check: P(yellow) = 8/20 = 2/5, and 3/5 + 2/5 = 1, as it must.

workedExamples.title: Practice 9
workedExamples.prompt: A coin is flipped and a die is rolled. List the sample space, then find P(heads and an odd number).
workedExamples.solution: Sample space: H1–H6, T1–T6 (12 outcomes). Heads with an odd number = H1, H3, H5 → P(heads and odd) = 3/12 = 1/4.

activities.title: The Coin-Flip Investigation
steps: Predict: how many heads do you expect in 10 flips? Write it down.
Flip the coin 10 times and tally the heads and tails.
Now flip it 40 more times so you have 50 flips in total, keeping the tally going.
Work out the experimental probability of heads after 10 flips and after 50 flips.
Which result is closer to the theoretical 1/2? Write a sentence explaining why, using the law of large numbers.

activities.title: Build a Bag of Chance
activities.materials: a cloth bag or bowl, and small objects of two or three colours (stones, beans, or bottle caps).
steps: Put in a known mixture, for example 5 red and 3 white – 8 objects in total.
Before drawing, calculate the theoretical P(red) and P(white).
Draw one object without looking, record its colour, and put it back. Do this 40 times.
Compare your experimental probabilities with the theoretical ones. How close are they?
Now ask a family member (or your AI tutor, if no one else is free) to secretly change the mixture, then use your experiments to guess the new amounts.

activities.title: Make a Paper Spinner
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and a paper clip or short stick as a pointer.
steps: Draw a circle and divide it into 8 equal sectors. Colour 4 green, 2 blue and 2 orange.
Write the theoretical probability of each colour as a fraction.
Spin the pointer 40 times (flick a paper clip held by a pencil at the centre) and tally the results.
Calculate the experimental probability of each colour.
Which colour was closest to its theoretical value? Design a 'fair' spinner where all three colours are equally likely.

activities.title: Two-Dice Totals Investigation
steps: List every total from 2 to 12. Predict which total you think will come up most often.
Roll the two die 50 times, each time adding the scores and tallying the total.
Make a bar of tallies for each total. Which total won?
Explain your result: there are 6 ways to make 7 but only 1 way to make 2 or 12.
Challenge: work out the theoretical probability of each total out of 36 and compare it to your tallies.

activities.title: The Fair-or-Unfair Detective (Family Game)
activities.materials: any everyday object with two outcomes – a bottle cap, a drawing pin, or a flat stone marked on one side.
steps: Choose an object and decide its two outcomes (for example, cap 'open up' or 'closed up').
Everyone guesses whether the object is fair (50/50) or unfair — if you are alone, guess by yourself or ask your AI tutor to make a guess too.
Drop or flip it 60 times as a group, or by yourself if no one else is available, tallying each outcome.
Calculate the experimental probability of each outcome.
Decide (together, or on your own) whether the evidence suggests the object is fair or unfair. Why do more trials make you more confident?

activities.title: Probability Around the Home (Investigation)
activities.materials: just your eyes and a notebook.
steps: Choose an event you can watch, for example 'the next car to pass is white' or 'the next person to enter wears sandals'.
Estimate the probability first, using the words impossible to certain and a fraction.
Observe 20 real examples and tally the outcomes.
Calculate the experimental probability and compare it with your estimate.
Write one sentence about what surprised you, and share it with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: What You Will Learn in This Unit
rules.text: By the end of this unit you will be able to place events on a probability scale from 0 to 1, calculate the probability of an event using fractions, decimals and percentages, list all the possible outcomes of an experiment in a sample space, and tell the difference between theoretical probability (what the mathematics predicts) and experimental probability (what actually happens when you try it). You will also learn about mutually exclusive events and a neat rule for finding the probability that something does *not* happen.

rules.title: The Complement Rule: P(not A) = 1 − P(A)
rules.text: Use the rule P(not A) = 1 − P(A) to find the probability an event does not happen.

rules.title: Probability Always Lies Between 0 and 1
rules.text: A very important rule follows from all this: a probability can never be bigger than 1 and never smaller than 0. If you ever calculate a probability of 1.5 or −0.2, you have made a mistake somewhere, because those numbers are off the scale. This is one of the fastest ways to check your own work. Whenever you finish a probability calculation, glance at the answer and ask: is it between 0 and 1? If not, go back.

rules.title: Why Use the Complement Rule
rules.text: Sometimes it is easier to work out the chance of an event not happening than the chance of it happening. There is a beautiful rule for this. Since all the probabilities in an experiment add up to 1, the probability that an event does not happen is 1 minus the probability that it does:

rules.title: Complement Rule Example
rules.text: For example, the probability of rolling a 6 on a die is 1/6, so the probability of not rolling a 6 is 1 − 1/6 = 5/6. This makes sense: five of the six faces are 'not a 6'. The 'not' event is called the complement, and the rule is one of the most useful shortcuts in probability, especially when the event you want is complicated but its opposite is simple. If Omar wants the probability of not drawing the winning raffle ticket, it is far quicker to work out the small chance of winning and subtract from 1.

rules.title: Adding Mutually Exclusive Probabilities
rules.text: So the probability of rolling a 2 or a 5 is P(2) + P(5) = 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 = 1/3. Likewise, drawing a marble that is 'red or yellow' from Khadija's bag (4 red, 3 blue, 1 yellow) is 4/8 + 1/8 = 5/8. The addition rule works here because no marble is both red and yellow at once.

commonMistakes: Writing only the favourable count as the probability instead of favourable ÷ total — e.g. saying P(red) = 4 instead of 4/10.
Adding P(A) + P(B) when A and B are not mutually exclusive double-counts the outcomes they share.
A probability must always be between 0 and 1 — if a calculation gives more than 1 (or less than 0), there is an error.
Believing that after several tails in a row, heads is 'due' next. Each fair flip is independent, so the probability stays 1/2 no matter what happened before.

A bag of sweets has P(mint) = 3/8. There are 24 sweets. How many are mints and how many are not?
A die is rolled 300 times. If it is fair, how many 5s would you expect? A student records 90 fives. What might this suggest, and why is 300 rolls more convincing than 30?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Expect 300 ÷ 6 = 50 fives; 90 is well above 50, suggesting possible bias; 300 rolls is more convincing than 30 because the law of large numbers means larger samples wander less from the true probability.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain why you may add the probabilities of 'rolling a 1' and 'rolling a 2', but you may not simply add the probabilities of 'rolling an even number' and 'rolling a number greater than 2'.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 'Rolling a 1' and 'rolling a 2' are mutually exclusive (cannot both happen), so their probabilities may be added; but 'even' and 'greater than 2' overlap (a 4 or 6 is both), so simply adding would count those outcomes twice.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Calculating Theoretical Probability.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Now we reach the heart of the unit: the formula for theoretical probability. When every outcome is equally likely, the probability of an event is the number of outcomes that make the event happen, divided by the total number of possible outcomes: P(event) = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of possible outcomes

rounds.explanation: On the probability scale, 0 means impossible and 1 means certain; 1.5 is not a valid probability at all.

rounds.prompt: A bag contains 4 red counters and 6 blue counters. One counter is drawn at random. What is P(red)?
rounds.clue: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.
rounds.explanation: P(red) = favourable ÷ total = 4/10 = 2/5.

One or more outcomes we are interested in
The set of all possible outcomes
rounds.answer: One possible result of an experiment
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 13 Math Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: Outcome means One possible result of an experiment.

rounds.prompt: Which word best describes the chance of rolling a 7 on an ordinary six-sided die?
rounds.clue: Work it out yourself first, then look for your answer among the options.
rounds.explanation: A standard die only has the faces 1 to 6, so a 7 can never appear — the event is impossible (probability 0).

rounds.prompt: A coin is flipped once. What is the sample space?
rounds.clue: Rule out the options you know are wrong, then check the one that is left.
rounds.explanation: A single coin flip has exactly two possible outcomes, so the sample space is {heads, tails}.

rounds.prompt: A fair die is rolled once. Are 'rolling a 2' and 'rolling a 5' mutually exclusive, and what is P(2 or 5)?
rounds.clue: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.
rounds.explanation: One roll cannot show both a 2 and a 5, so the events are mutually exclusive; P(2 or 5) = 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 = 1/3.

rounds.prompt: A bag holds only red, blue and green balls. P(red) = 0.3 and P(blue) = 0.45. Since red, blue and green are mutually exclusive and cover every ball, what is P(green)?
rounds.clue: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.
rounds.explanation: Mutually exclusive probabilities that cover every outcome add to 1: P(green) = 1 − 0.3 − 0.45 = 0.25.

selfAssessment: I can describe how likely an event is using the words impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely and certain.
I can place events on a probability scale from 0 to 1 and read values off it.
I can express a probability as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage, and convert between them.
I can list the sample space – all the possible outcomes – of a simple experiment.
I can calculate theoretical probability using P(event) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes.
I can use the rule P(not A) = 1 − P(A) to find the probability an event does not happen.
I can recognise mutually exclusive events and add their probabilities.
